en: Majjhima Nikāya 16,
Cetokhila Sutta:
Thus have I heard—
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus!”
“Venerable Sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One said this:
“Bhikkhus, for whatever bhikkhu the five mental deserts have not been abandoned, and the five mental shackles...”
"It is impossible that one who has not severed these [five mental barrennesses] will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.
What five mental barrennesses have he not abandoned?
Here, monks, a monk is doubtful, perplexed, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the Teacher.
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Teacher, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
Since his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this first wilderness of the mind remains unabandoned by him.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence in the Dhamma … [and so on] …”
In this way, this second wilderness of the mind remains unabandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk doubts, is perplexed, is not resolved, and does not have confidence in the Saṅgha ... [as before] ...
in this way, this third wilderness of the mind remains unabandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the training.
For that monk who is doubtful, uncertain, undecided, and lacks confidence regarding the training, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
Since his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fourth mental barrenness remains unabandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is angry with his companions in the holy life, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring a grudge.

Monks, for that monk who is angry with his companions in the holy life, displeased, with a resentful mind, and harboring a grudge, his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental barrenness remains unabandoned.
These five mental barrennesses have not been abandoned by him.
What five mental shackles have not been severed by him?

Here, monks, a monk is not free from lust for sensual pleasures; he has not departed from desire, not departed from affection, not departed from thirst, not departed from fever, and not departed from craving for them.

“Monks, when a monk is not free from lust for sensual pleasures, not free from desire, not free from affection, not free from thirst, not free from fever, and not free from craving for them, his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving, this first mental fetter remains unsevered.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not free from lust for the body … [and so on] …”
In this way, this second mental fetter remains unsevered for him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not free from lust for forms...
[as before] ...in this way, this third mental fetter remains unsevered for him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk eats as much as he likes until his belly is full and dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness. Monks,
for that monk who eats as much as he likes until his belly is full and dwells devoted to the pleasure of lying down, the pleasure of reclining, and the pleasure of drowsiness,
his mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
In one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fourth mental bond remains unsevered.
Furthermore, monks, a monk leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas, thinking:
"By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a deva or some kind of deva."
“Bhikkhus, when a bhikkhu leads the holy life aspiring for some order of devas,
thinking: ‘By this virtue, or observance, or asceticism, or holy life, may I become a deva or some kind of deva,’ his mind does not incline toward ardor, commitment, perseverance, and striving.”
For one whose mind does not incline toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental shackle remains unsevered.
These five mental shackles remain unsevered for him.
Monks, for any monk who has not abandoned these five wildernesses of the heart and these five mental shackles...

“Bhikkhus, it is impossible that a bhikkhu who has not severed the five kinds of mental barrenness will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline. But, bhikkhus, it is possible that a bhikkhu for whom the five kinds of mental barrenness have been abandoned and the five fetters of the mind have been well severed will attain growth, increase, and fulfillment in this Dhamma and Discipline.”
What are his five mental barrennesses that have been abandoned?
Here, monks, a monk does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has confidence in the Teacher.
Monks, for that monk who does not doubt, does not waver, is resolved, and has confidence in the Teacher, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, in this way his first mental barrenness is abandoned.
Furthermore, monks, when a monk does not doubt, is not perplexed, is resolved, and has confidence in the Dhamma … [as before] … in this way his second mental barrenness is abandoned.
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not doubt, is not perplexed, is resolved, and has full confidence in the Saṅgha … [as before] … Thus this third mental barrenness is abandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not doubt, is not perplexed, is resolved, and has full confidence in the training … [as before] …
In this way, this fourth mental wasteland is abandoned by him.
Furthermore, monks, a monk is not angry toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life, nor is he displeased, nor is his mind struck down, nor has he become callous.

Monks, for that monk who is not angry toward his fellow practitioners of the holy life, nor displeased, nor struck down in mind, nor callous, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
When his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, then this fifth mental barrenness has been abandoned by him.
These five mental barrennesses have been abandoned by him.
What five mental shackles has he completely severed?
"Here, monks, a monk is free from lust for sensual pleasures; he is devoid of desire, devoid of affection, devoid of thirst, devoid of fever, and devoid of craving.
For that monk, monks, who is free from lust for sensual pleasures and devoid of desire, affection, thirst, fever, and craving, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this first mental fetter is thoroughly severed."
Furthermore, monks, a bhikkhu is free from lust for the body … free from lust for forms … he does not eat as much as he likes until his belly is full,
nor does he dwell addicted to the pleasure of sleep, the pleasure of lying down, or the pleasure of drowsiness.
“Monks, when a monk does not eat as much as he likes until his belly is full, and does not dwell devoted to the pleasure of lying down,
the pleasure of reclining, or the pleasure of sloth, his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fourth mental bond is thoroughly severed.”
Furthermore, monks, a monk does not lead the holy life aspiring for any particular class of gods, thinking:
"By this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, may I become a god or some other kind of god.
That monk, monks, who does not lead the holy life aspiring for any particular class of gods...
‘By means of this virtue, or vow, or austerity, or holy life, I shall become a god or one of the higher gods’—
his mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving.
For one whose mind inclines toward ardor, devotion, perseverance, and striving, this fifth mental fetter is thoroughly severed.
These five mental shackles of his have been thoroughly severed.

Monks, for whatever monk these five mental barrennesses have been abandoned and these five mental shackles have been thoroughly severed, it is possible that he will attain growth, increase, and maturity in this Dhamma and Discipline. This is the possibility.
Thus, he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of desire and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving.
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration due to investigation and volitional formations of striving; this is the fifth exertion.
Monks, a monk who is thus endowed with these fifteen factors of exertion is capable of breaking out, capable of awakening, capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
It is just as if, monks, there were a hen’s eggs—eight, ten, or twelve.
Suppose those eggs were properly incubated by that hen, properly warmed, and properly nurtured.
Even though it might not occur to that hen to wish:
“Oh, may these chicks break open the eggshells with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and hatch safely!”
“Then those chicks would indeed be capable of breaking out of their eggshells with the tips of their claws or with their beaks and emerging safely.
In the same way, monks, a monk who possesses these fifteen factors of exertion is capable of breaking out, capable of awakening, and capable of attaining the unsurpassed security from bondage.
This is what the Blessed One said.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the Blessed One’s words.
The sixth sutta, "The Barrenness of Mind," is finished.
